Notes: First documented Jewish presence: in the 1805 household register only one of 816 registered families (7482 people) was Jewish (Enoch Sertkovich and his wife Dvorka). Estimate based on families (1 family x5).
6th revision (1811): 66 souls of Jewish meshchane (townsmen estate) registered in Taganrog; covers one estate only, so not used as total population
66 Jewish meshchane lived in Taganrog 'not counting members of their families' - count of heads only, total unknown
Oldest Jewish cemetery in the region, with first graves older than 1813
1837 register kept by Rostov rabbi Vulf Kalina (whose congregants included Taganrog Jews) recorded 24 boys and 17 girls born - vital events, not population
Kh.-E. Vaks was rabbi in Taganrog 1841-1862

178 officially registered Jewish families lived in Taganrog in 1845 (37 merchants and 141 meshchane); estimate based on families. By 27 March 1845 a synagogue, prayer school and burial society functioned
Jewish population counted 413 persons in 1847 (source also states the community numbered 178 families around 1845)
A Jewish prayer house functioned already in the first decades of the 19th century; a synagogue building was built in 1848; in 1846 collector Yakov Brailovsky initiated building a synagogue
In 1850 Taganrog Jews recorded 28 boys and 17 girls born, 14 marriages and 20 deaths - vital events, not population
748 Jews lived in Taganrog in 1859
Jewish population reached 577 persons in 1859 (differs from other sources giving 748)
Synagogue construction (permission Feb 1859) completed in rough form in 1861; rebuilt 1873-1876
In the 1860s a synagogue with a choir was built (year = midpoint of the 1860s)
Two-storey brick choral synagogue completed in 1876
Taganrog incorporated in the Don Army region beyond the Pale of Settlement; new Jewish settlement forbidden, only previous residents allowed to stay
1897 census: 2960 Jews (6% of total population)
At the turn of the century 4030 Jews lived in Taganrog (year = turn of century as stated by source)
During the 1905 revolution a meeting of Jewish voters held in the synagogue drew 450 people - attendance, not population
Second Jewish prayer house opened 12 September 1910
In 1917 the Jewish population of Taganrog reached 8000
Synagogue building nationalized 23 April 1923 (choral synagogue closed)
More than 600 Jewish families in the city at the time of the 1924 attempt to found a religious society (300+ Jews petitioned); estimate based on families
'700 Jewish families in Taganrog, half of them working people' in the 1920s; estimate based on families; year = midpoint of 1920s
1926 census: 2673 Jews (about 3%)
1939 census: 3124 Jews

By October 1941 the number of Jews was about 7000 due to refugees; Jews were ordered to assemble on 26 Oct 1941, up to 1800 were collected at a school and shot on 30 Oct; officially 6975 people died in the Petrushino 'Balka of death' (10000-12000 by other data, not only Jews). Refugee-inflated estimate and death tolls not used as population. Source also says Jews were no more than 1% of the population before

29 October 1941: all Jews of Taganrog (around 2500 people) gathered on Vladimirskaya Plaza and shot in the Gully of Petrushino by Einsatzgruppe D collaborators; ~7000 Taganrogers killed there in total. Victim count, not population
On 29 October 1941 the Germans shot 1500 to 3000 Taganrog Jews - death toll
During the 1941-1943 occupation the Nazis killed about 10000 people including more than 6500 Jews (1500 children) - death toll
All Jews who did not manage to escape were killed during the German occupation
Jewish community formally established in 1996 on the basis of the 'Lechaim' Jewish culture society
By 2005 the new community had a community center, youth, women's and veterans' clubs, Sunday school, burial society and Holocaust educational center
In 2012 the community (led by Tankha Otershteyn) sought land for a new synagogue
